*vieles*German{}|Alternative forms}Vieles|Etymology}Neuter singular form of viel.|Pronunciation}/ˈfiːləs/}Ⓓe/ec/De-@^.ogg|Pronoun}#much,many things}•'''Vieles''' hat sich in den letzten Jahren verändert.}•Much has changed over the past years.}#}• Die Kirche erklärt mit Recht als Selige im Himmel diejenigen  welche des Evangeliums wegen '''Vieles''' gelitten haben ...|Usage notes}Formal standard German distinguishes the indefinite pronouns viel and ''@^'',both translating as “much”. More precisely,however,the former means “much of one sort of thing”,whereas the latter means “many different things”. For example:''Ich habe viel gegessen.'' → “I ate a large quantity of food”. ''Ich habe @^ gegessen.'' → “I ate a great variety of foods”. The distinction may be lost in colloquial German,where ''@^'' is seldom used at all.}''Vieles'' changes to ''vielem'' in the dative case. A genitive form does not exist. It needs to be paraphrased by means of the preposition von.

Further in all likelihood a folk-etymological alteration of from Old Norse litmountain cat,from tmountain+ttomcat.}Further discussion}The Old Norse origin has been disputed because from Norwegian twolverine is only found in local dialects and is attested later than the Middle Low German. Moreover,the German form was later borrowed into from Danish - and from Swedish - (see descendants below). The usual Scandinavian word for the animal is from Norwegian jerv,from Danish jærv,from Swedish järv. Nevertheless,the etymology is now generally accepted on semantic grounds. The popular belief that the wolverine is particularly voracious only developed because of the name,not vice versa. Additionally,the existence of the Middle Low German forms in ''-s,-tz'' supports the derivation,because in a native compound we should expect only ''-t'' (and a borrowing from High German into Low German is not plausible for a Scandinavian animal in the 15th century).}{{rel-bottom|Noun}(mask.)}#wolverine,glutton Literally:[taxfmt]}#}• Hierdurch bekundet der ausgezeichnete Naturforscher  was der '''@^''' ist:ein Mittelglied zwischen den genannten Familien. *vogelfrei*German{}|Etymology}15th century,from Vogel,(bird)frei,(free). The earliest use was of persons who were free from feudal obligation and thus enjoyed freedom of movement. It seems plausible that the use for “outlawed” may be based on this,in the sense that the outlaw is forced ever to move from place to place. However,the predominantly accepted derivation is from the fact that outlaws could not be buried in Christian cemeteries and were left,as it were,to the birds. Perhaps both notions have contributed.|Pronunciation}/ˈfoːɡəlˌfraɪ̯/+ˈfoːɡl̩ˌfʁaɪ̯ usually in the sense “outlawed”}Ⓓ1/13/De-@^.ogg}/ˈfoːɡəlˈfraɪ̯/+ˈfoːɡl̩ˈfʁaɪ̯ usually in the sense “free as a bird”|Adjective}#outlawed,banished,proscribed Literally:[stripped of all rights and allowed to be killed]}•synononym:[geächtet],[gebannt],[rechtlos],[entrechtet]}#fairly free as a bird}#}• Er fühlte sich '''@^'''  zum ersten Male ein Mann  der sich auf seinen eigenen Willen lehne.}(He felt '''free as a bird''')  for the first time a man who might rely on his own will.|Descendants}desctree:cal1

One uses  when both the places “from which” and “''to'' which” are given:''Dieser Zug fährt '''&_''' Köln nach Hamburg.'' – “This train goes from Cologne to Hamburg.” If the further direction is not given,''aus'' is the normal choice:''Dieser Zug kommt '''aus''' Köln.'' – “This train is coming from Cologne.” The phrase:''Dieser Zug kommt &_ Köln'' is not wrong but has a colloquial ring to it.}sense:of The preposition  is used to replace possessive and partitive genitives,sometimes also prepositions that govern the genitive. Such replacement can be obligatory,optional,or restricted to the glossary:colloquial register:}:It is obligatory if the genitive cannot be expressed grammatically,which is the case with common nouns not preceded by any declinable glossary:articles,glossary:determiners,or glossary:adjectives:''die Rechte &_ Kindern'' (“children’s rights”); ''der Geschmack &_ Käse'' (“the taste of cheese”). This is also true of most singular,demonstrative pronouns and often true of all personal pronouns:''der Geschmack &_ diesem'' (“the taste of this”); ''ein Freund &_ mir'' (“a friend of mine”);  is archaic in modern German.}:The replacement is optional in cases such as the following:

Since both of these would normally be spelled ⟨@^⟩,depending on time and region,it cannot be told from the records which one was thought of as the Middle Low German supraregional standard,nor whether the two pronunciations were associated with different meanings.|Prefix}#modyfying verb-prefix,denoting amongst other things intent towards something or intensification}•''vorspreken'' (to promise) from ''spreken'' (to speak),''vorgeven'' (to forgive)}#denotes an action with a negative result such as destruction,loss or spoilage}•''vordarven'' (to rot),''vorlysen'' (to lose)}#denotes an action flawed with a mistake}•''vorscriven'' (to make a mistake in writing) from ''scriven'' (to write)|Derived terms}prefixsee:gml

*Vorzeitigkeit*German{}|Etymology}From vorzeitig+-keit.|Noun}(fem.)}#the state of being premature}#grammar pre-timeliness; antecedent|Usage notes}In grammar,describes the relationship of different grammatical tenses in main and subordinate clauses,in which the action of the subordinate clause takes place before that of the main clause. For instance,in the sentence "''Ich schlafe,nachdem ich meine Hausaufgaben gemacht habe.''" ("I sleep after I've done my homework."),the word nachdem is used to create the pre-timeliness:The subordinate clause ("I've done my homework") takes place before that of the main clause ("I sleep").|Coordinate terms}Gleichzeitigkeit,Nachzeitigkeit

*wahnsinnig*German{}|Etymology}Coined in the 15th century after the model of wahnwitzig which uses as its first part the word wahn,which came from Old High German wan "missing,empty",which came from Proto-Germanic ⋆wanaz. Not cognate with Wahn. *Wal*German{}|Etymology}The root descends from Middle High German - and from Old High German wal,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hwal,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hwalaz,from Proto-Indo-European sheatfish. Cognates include from English whale,from German Low German Waal,from Icelandic hvalur,from Danish hval,from Swedish val.}Although the simplex root also existed in earlier historical stages of German,Grimm claims that the simplex had fallen out of used by Early New High German and was used exclusively in the compounds such as &_fisch and Narwal. The simplex later reappeared in the course of the 19th century,at first in the domain of scientific literature,as a from German nocap1. Compare also from Dutch walvis,from Low German Waalfisch.|Pronunciation}/vaːl/}Ⓓe/ee/De-&_.ogg}Wahl}Rhymes:aːl|Noun}(mask.,plural:[&_(e)s])}#whale}•synononym:[&_fisch],[qdated]|Derived terms}col-auto:&_rat

*Warte*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German warte,from Old High German warta,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆wardu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆wardō.|Pronunciation}ˈvaɐ̯tə+ˈvaʁtə}Ⓓd/df/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#lookout,guarding post}#figurative point of view,perspective,side}#}• Der BGH sieht daher unter Zustimmung eines Teils der Literatur alle MM als reine ''Unrechtselemente'' an. Diese Zuordnung wird auch durch die normative Schuldtheorie nahe gelegt  zu der sich nicht nur der BGH  sondern auch die überwiegende Auffassung im Schrifttum bekennt. Charakteristisch für sie ist es  Schuld bloß durch ein negatives Kriterium  nämlich dem Zurückbleiben hinter den Verhaltensanforderungen des Rechts zu bestimmen. Von dieser '''@^''' aus stehen dann alle Motive und Absichten  die zum Töten führen einander gleich und können daher keine Schuldelemente aufweisen.}#}• Es gewähren die §§ 994 I 1  995 BGB dem gutgläubigen Besitzer Ersatz für notwendige Verwendungen unabhängig von einem verbleibendem Verwendungserfolg. Sie zielen mithin auf den Ausgleich einer Entreicherung und ''nicht'' auf die Abschöpfung einer Bereicherung (anders § 818 III); … Nicht notwendige Verwendungen werden ihm dagegen nur insoweit ersetzt  als sie den Wert der Sache auch noch im Zeitpunkt ihrer Rückgabe erhöhen  § 996. Dies begründet zwar das Risiko einer aufgedrängten Bereicherung; da aber das Vermögen des Eigentümers hierdurch nicht geschmälert wird (Vermögensumschichtung  nicht aber -reduktion)  erscheint es angemessen  dem Vertrauensschutz insoweit (noch) den Vorrang einzuräumen. Verwendungen  die sich aus der '''@^''' des Eigentümers (bei entsprechender Ersatzpflicht) jedoch als vermögensreduzierend darstellen (weder notwendig noch nützlich)  sind hingegen nicht ersatzfähig.

*was*German{}|Alternative forms}wat|Etymology}From Middle High German waz,from Old High German waz,from Old High German hwaz,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hwat,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆kʷod. Cognate with from Bavarian &_,from Bavarian wås,woas (from East Central German &_),from Dutch wat,from English what,from Danish hvad. from German wat.|Pronunciation}/vas/}Ⓓ5/56/DE-&_.ogg}Ⓓ/b/ba/BY-&_.ogg(Bavaria)(Bavaria)}Rhymes:as|Pronoun}#interrogative what}•'''Was''' machst du heute?}•'''What''' are you doing today?}#relative which (referring to the entire preceding clause)}•Sie tanzte gut,'''&_''' er bewunderte.}•She &_ a good dancer,'''which''' he admired.}#relative that,which (referring to m+de+das,alles,et&_,nichts,and neuter substantival adjectives)}•Das ist alles,'''&_''' ich weiß.}•That's all '''that''' I know.}•Das ist das Beste,'''&_''' mir passieren konnte.}•That's the best '''that''' could have happened to me.}#relative that,which (referring to neuter singular nouns,instead of standard m+de+das)}•Siehst du das weiße Haus,'''&_''' renoviert wird?}•Do you see that white house,'''which''' is being renovated?}#indefinite something,anything (instead of standard m+de+et&_)}•Ich hab '''&_''' gefunden.}•I've found '''something'''.}#}• Er wollte Anna '''&_''' antun. (He wanted to do something to Anna.)}#interrogative why (with emphasis,astonishment or disapproval)}•'''Was''' birgst du so bang dein Gesicht?}•'''Why on earth''' are you hiding your face so fearfully?|Usage notes}''Was'' is colloquially used with prepositions,chiefly but not exclusively in southern regions. Otherwise it is generally replaced with a pronominal adverb containing wo- (or in a few cases wes-). Hence:,instead of '''''Mit &_''' hast du das gemacht?'',and weswegen instead of ''wegen &_''.}The genitive case,and the dative case if necessary for clearness,can be paraphrased by means of welcher Sache. Possessive genitives are more commonly paraphrased with wovon. It is also possible to use the genitive form ,but it wouldn't be used in questions such as '''''Wessen''' ist das?'' because here it would be understood as the genitive form of wer.}The colloquial ''&_'' meaning "something" can only be the first word in a sentence if followed by an adjective: Otherwise the full form ''et&_'' must be used: The reason for this is that the latter sentence could be misinterpreted as a question if ''&_'' were used.|Derived terms}komme,&_ wolle}&_ ist dir; &_ ist Dir}&_ kostet es}&_ zum Geier; &_ zum Kuckuck}tun,&_ man nicht lassen kann}&_ auch immer}&_ der Bauer nicht kennt,das frisst er nicht}&_ geht}&_ gibt's Neues}&_ du nicht sagst; &_ ihr nicht sagt; &_ Sie nicht sagen|Determiner}#archaic what; what kind of}•synononym:&_ für}#}• ... denen Thieren und Gewächsen aber  von '''&_''' Arten und Geschlechten selbige auch nur immer seyn mögen  ...}#}&_ Held August,du kühner Krieger!/Du bist der beglückte Sieger,/Vor,und in,und nach dem Fall./Auf '''&_''' Arten,auf '''&_''' Weisen,/Soll man deine Thaten preisen/Hier und da,und überall?}#}&_ Wie und auf '''&_''' Weise jedermann seinen ... Nebenmenschen Hülfe leisten ... solle.|Usage notes}In the dative and genitive feminine,the inflected form &_er occurred.|Adverb}#colloquial et&_}•Ich komm '''&_''' später.}•I'll arrive '''a little''' later.}#interrogative why,what for}•synononym:[warum],[wieso],[weshalb]}•'''Was''' bist du heute so stumm?}•'''Why''' are you so silent today?||Low German{}|Verb}#inflection of:indc}#inflection of:indc}#apocopated form of m:&_h,inflection of:impr qualifier:mainly used in the Netherlands,equivalent to other dialects' &_che/&_ke}#apocopated form of m:wax,inflection of:impr}#apocopated form of m:grow,inflection of:impr|Usage notes}Notes on the verb ''węsen'' (to be):In recent times (~1800) the old subjunctive ''wer'' is used in place of ''&_'' by many speakers. This might be the old subjunctive which is now used as a preterite or a reduction of ''weren'',which is the preterite plural indicative of the verb. It might also be an imitation of the High German cognate ''war''. Many smaller dialectal clusters do this,but no dialect does it. That means:even though there are many regions within e.g. Lower Saxony that use ''wer'' for ''&_'',maybe even the majority,there is no straight connection between them,i.e. which form is used can depend on preference,speaker and specific region. Due to this "one town this way,one town that way"-nature of the situation no form can be named "standard" for a greater dialect,such as Low Saxon.||Middle Low German{}|Alternative forms}&_s|Verb}#Form of [wēsen]||Old High German{}|Alternative forms}uuas|Verb}#Form of [wesan]||Pennsylvania German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German waz,from Old High German waz,from Old High German hwaz,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hwat.}Compare from German &_,from Dutch wat,from English what.|Pronoun}#interrogative what

*wegen*German{}|Etymology}Shortened version of ,from Middle High German von+genitive object+@^,with from Middle High German @^ being the dative plural of from Middle High German wec,modern-day Weg,but with a meaning similar to Ort,Stelle,Seite.|Pronunciation}/ˈveːɡən/+/ˈveːɡŋ̩/}Ⓓ1/1f/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓc/c1/De-@^2.ogg}we+gen|Preposition}@^ ( with  genqq:standard/datqq:informal,or standardly in certain circumstances)}#for,because of}•'''Wegen''' des schlechten Wetters werden wir zu Hause bleiben.}•'''Because of''' the bad weather,we will stay at home.|Usage notes}'''1.)''' While use with the dative is now considered acceptable in informal use,it is still considered erroneous by conservative or linguistically aware speakers (except in certain cases,see below). In the '''standard language''',''@^'' is usually followed by the original genitive:}:}Die Autobahn wurde @^ '''eines Unfalls''' gesperrt.}•The autobahn was closed because of an accident.}:Even in formal language,the dative case is normally used if the genitive would be indistinguishable from the nominative in form,which is the case with plural nouns not preceded by an article,determiner,or adjective:}:}Die Autobahn wurde @^ '''Unfällen''' gesperrt.}•The autobahn was closed because of accidents.}:The dative case is also used with pronouns whose genitive form is not heard as often,and if a possessive genitive is preceding the referent of the preposition.}:}Er rief @^ '''etwas Wichtigem''' an.}•He called because of something important.}:}Er rief @^ Peters '''neuem Auto''' an.}•He called because of Peter's new car. (→ ''@^ Peters neuen Autos'' is possible,but unusual)}:Masculine and neuter singular nouns not preceded by an article,determiner,or adjective may take inflectional -''(e)s'',although this is now quite formal. Personal names never take an ending.}:}Er war @^ '''Fieber'''('''s''') verhindert.}•He was unavailable because of a fever.}:}Sie ist @^ '''Anton''' nach Köln gezogen.}•She moved to Cologne because of Anton.}:Personal pronouns and some other pronouns have special contracted forms with ''@^'':}:}meinet@^,deinet@^,seinet@^,ihret@^,unseret@^,euret@^}:}dessent@^,derent@^,wessent@^,weß@^ (dated)}'''2.)''' In the '''vernacular''',and occasionally in writing,it is common to use the dative case after ''@^'' at all times,whereby all the above peculiarities cease to apply. To some,the genitive may even sound pretentious in a private conversation. This is long-standing practice in the German dialects,which have mostly abolished the genitive per se.}:}Die Autobahn wurde @^ '''einem Unfall''' gesperrt.}•The autobahn was closed because of an accident.}'''3.)''' In very formal usage,''@^'' may be used as a postposition (always with genitive).}:}Die Autobahn wurde '''eines Unfalls @^''' gesperrt.}•The autobahn was closed because of an accident.

Gebrauch von patronym. lang:-ειος bei ''o''-Stämmen,ist eine Neuerung; dieses lang:-ειος ist als Universalsuffix auch bei Kons.-Stämmen verwendet; und es stammt als ''-ios''-Ableitung von den Namen auf lang:-ης,so lang:-ειος neben lang:-ης in Thessalien,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης als lang:-εις geschrieben) l. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; auf Lesbos patronym. 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,'''@^''' 621,11 als Name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; das Muster für mask. lang:-γένειος usw. war vermutlich nicht-patronym. fem. lang:-εια (hom. lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια oder lang:-κλέεια).|The main evidence for Greek lang:-ειος,the Aeolic use of patronymic lang:-ειος with ''o''-stems,is an innovation; this lang:-ειος is used as a universal suffix with consonant stems; and it derives from nouns in lang:-ης as a ''-ios''-derivation,thus lang:-ειος is near lang:-ης in Thessaly,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης written as lang:-εις) vid. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; patronymic on Lesbos 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,'''fem.''' 621,11 as the name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; the example for the masculine lang:-γένειος etc. was presumably the non-patronymic fem. lang:-εια (Homeric lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια or lang:-κλέεια).

*Weihnachten*German{}|Alternative forms}@-2 literary|Etymology}From Middle High German Christmas,from a dative plural in the holy nights. Compare modern weihen and Nacht.}The oldest form (1170) is a singular ''diu wīhe naht'' (“the Holy Night”); the somewhat later plural is used to refer to the Christmas days and nights collectively. A relation with earlier heathen festivals is not endorsed by the etymological standard sources,though the possibility is admitted.}The term is a cognate with from Low German Wiehnachten as well as from Czech Vánoce and from Slovak Vianoce.|Pronunciation}/ˈvaɪ̯ˌnaxtən/+ˈväɪ̯ˌnäχtən+ˈʋäɪ̯-+-ˌnäχtn̩}Ⓓf/fe/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(neut.,genitive:@^s,plural:[@^])}#often Christmas}•synononym:[@-2sfest],[Christfest]}•Es ist '''@^.'''}•It's Christmas.}•frohe @^}•frohe '''@^'''! (fröhliche @^}•fröhliche '''@^'''!)}•merry Christmas!}•wir}•Wir wünschen Ihnen frohe '''@^''' und ein gutes neues Jahr!}•(''formal'') We wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!}#}'''2016''',Miriam Malik,''Ein Drache zu @^ und andere @-2sgeschichten'',story ''Ein Löwe zu @^'':}#}:Drei '''@^''',zwei Ostern und Fasching sowie unzählige Kindergeburtstage hatte ich bereits überstanden.+I already endured three ''Christmases'',two Easters and carnival as well as countless child's birthdays.|Usage notes}In German-speaking countries,'''@^''' includes the 25th as well as the 26th of December and usually also the evening of the 24th (from circa 6 p.m.). The inclusion of the morning and afternoon of the 24th is informal and sometimes frowned upon.}'''@^''' is originally a plurale tantum with the singular meaning ''Christmas''. This is still invariably used in wishes:''Frohe,gesegnete,schöne,... '''@^'''!'' Otherwise,the word is most often treated as a neuter singular:'''''@^''' ist ein christliches Fest.'' (“Christmas is a Christian holiday.”) Particularly in Austria and Switzerland,the plurale tantum may alternatively be used,then requiring the definite article:''Die '''@^''' sind ein christliches Fest.'' The neuter singular also has a true plural referring to Christmases in different years:''Die letzten drei '''@^''' war er krank.'' *weil*German{}|Etymology}From the accusative of from Middle High German wīle (modern Weile),from Old High German wīla,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hwīlu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hwīlō.|Pronunciation}/vaɪ̯l/}Ⓓb/b8/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓf/fe/De-@^2.ogg}Ⓓ1/1e/De-@^3.ogg}Ⓓ/7/73/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Rhymes:aɪ̯l|Conjunction}#because,given that}•Ich kann nicht kommen,'''@^''' ich krank bin.}•I can't come '''because''' I'm sick.}#archaic while,during|Usage notes}In standard German,''@^'' is a subordinating conjunction and links a subordinate clause with the conjugated verb in the final position: At the beginning of a sentence,some style guides prefer replacing ''@^'' with da:}In spontaneous speech,is also used as a coordinating conjunction by linking a second independent clause with the conjugated verb in the second position: Here,functions similarly to denn: In writing which imitates speech (such as texting),this same phenomenon can be observed.}It is possible that  is currently undergoing a process of re-grammaticalization in which it can be used like da or denn; that is,as a subordinating or coordinating conjunction. From 1955 to 1974,only 8.3% of -clauses in spontaneous speech were verb-second,yet by 1993 to 2000,this had increased to 46.6%. If such a process is underway,it is far from complete:Usage of  as a coordinating conjunction with a verb-second word order remains nonstandard and is virtually non-existent in formal written German.

*welcher*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German welich,from Old High German welih,from Old High German wilih,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hwilīkaz. Compare from English which.|Pronunciation}/ˈvɛlçər/+ˈvɛl.çɐ+ˈvɛʎ-+ˈvɛɪ̯-+ʋ-}Ⓓ0/00/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ0/02/De-@^2.ogg|Determiner}#interrogative which; what}•'''Welche''' Farbe hat dein Kleid?}•'''What''' colour is your dress?}•'''Welches''' Buch in diesem Regal hast du am öftesten gelesen?}•'''Which''' book on this shelf have you read most often?}#relative which}•Er vergaß,die letzte Kugel aus dem Lauf zu nehmen,'''@^''' Fehler ihn das Leben kosten würde.}•He forgot to remove the last bullet from the barrel,a mistake '''which''' would cost him his life.|Pronoun}#interrogative which (one)}•Hier sind zwei Jacken,'''@-1''' ist deine?}•There are two jackets here,'''which one''' is yours?}#relative that; which; who; whom}•Der Mann,'''@-1n''' sie als ihren Nachbarn erkannte,lag tot auf dem Bürgersteig.}•The man,'''whom''' she recognized to be her neighbour,was lying dead on the pavement.}#indefinite some Literally:[an unspecified amount of]}•Soll ich Butter mitbringen oder ist noch '''@-1''' im Kühlschrank?}•Shall I bring butter or is there still '''some''' in the fridge?|Usage notes}When used as an interrogative determiner,some speakers may consider ''@^'' rather formal and may use was für instead,e.g. ''Was für eine Farbe hat dein Kleid?'' instead of ''Welche Farbe hat dein Kleid?''}When ''@^'' isn't used as a determiner followed directly by a noun (''Welche'' Farbe ist deine Lieblingsfarbe?) and is directly followed by the verb ''sein'',it is mostly used in neutral form ''@-1s'' for all genders and plural (Welches ist deine Lieblingsfarbe?). When it agrees with the gender and number,it is usually meant as one from a number of given options (Welche (von diesen) ist deine Lieblingsfarbe?)}''Welcher'' as a relative pronoun is virtually never used in the vernacular. It occurs more often in literary German,but overusing it is a typical trait of a pretentious style (generally corrected by editors). The normal relative pronoun in all registers of German is der and its forms.}''Welcher'' and its forms may be used avoid a doubled word. For example}:''Das Lied,@-1s das Kind vortrug,wurde vor langer Zeit geschrieben.''}:avoids ''das das''. The ''@-1s'' version would still not be preferred in general though.}German does not distinguish between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses and relies solely on context to determine which is meant. (See the usage notes at m:which.) Thus der and its forms are still preferred when English prefers "which":}:Paul schenkt sein Auto,das noch neu ist,seiner Tochter.}•Paul is giving his car,which is still new,to his daughter.

*wenig*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German weinec,from Middle High German marginal,from Old High German ⋆weinag,from Old High German miserable,from Proto-Germanic ⋆wainagaz. The form with from Old High German -ei- is original; that with from Old High German -ē- arose through conflation with the morphologically simpler Old High German from Old High German woe,akin to from English woe. The diphthong from Old High German -ei- later on regularly became from Old High German -ē- in several dialects,which further strengthened the monophthongal form . Cognate with from Dutch weinig,from Hunsrik wenich,from Yiddish ווייניק.}The comparative  comes from Middle High German minder,from Middle High German minre,from Middle High German minner; the from Middle High German - superlative is from Middle High German minnest,from Middle High German minst. Both are related to from Middle High German min.|Pronunciation}/ˈveːnɪç/,(standard) northern and central Germany}/ˈveːnɪk/,(standard) southern Germany,Austria,Switzerland}Ⓓ5/50/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓf/ff/De-@^2.ogg}Ⓓ/d/de/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)|Adjective}#little,few Literally:[a small amount,a small number]|Usage notes}The irregular compared forms ''minder,am mindesten'' are now restricted to formal usage where they are still commonly found as adverbs,chiefly in negation and especially when modifying adjectives. For example:''nicht minder gefährlich'' – "no less dangerous",alongside:''nicht @^er gefährlich''. Otherwise,only the regular forms are now commonly used.

*Wespe*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German wefse,from Middle High German webse,from Middle High German wespe,from Old High German wefsa. The forms with ''-sp-'' come from Middle Low German wespe,from Old Saxon waspa (10th century,alongside older from Old Saxon wepsia),spreading to Middle High German in the 12th century.}Some Upper German dialects retain the original consonantism to this day,e.g. from Swabian Wefz,from Bavarian Weps,from Bavarian Wepsn,from Bavarian Webasn,from Bavarian Webes. The spread of ''-sp-'' was reinforced,if not triggered,by from Latin vespa. Popular association with the verb wispeln from Old High German to whir,to whisper is also likely; compare from Central Franconian wasp. Both the High German and the Low German forms go back to from Proto-West Germanic ⋆waspijā,a variant of from Proto-West Germanic ⋆wapsu.}Cognates include from Dutch wesp,from English wasp,from French guêpe. These are often traced back to from Proto-Germanic ⋆wapsō,from Proto-Indo-European wasp,pertaining to from Proto-Indo-European to weave. There are some formal problems to this particular reconstruction,however,most importantly the fact that from Proto-Germanic ⋆wapsō is an anomalous form lacking the expected effect of Primärberührung.|Pronunciation}/ˈvɛspə/}Ⓓ6/67/De-@^.ogg}Wes+pe|Noun}(fem.)}#wasp Literally:[insect]|Hyponyms}Gallwespe,Kleinwespe,Schlupfwespe

*willkommen*German{}|Etymology}from Middle High German willekomen,from Old High German willechomen,from Proto-Germanic ⋆wiljakumô. Cognate to from Dutch welkom,from English welcome,from Danish velkommen,and other Germanic forms. Cognate with from Portuguese bem-vindo,from French bienvenu,from Italian benvenuto,from Spanish bienvenido,possibly Germanic calques.|Pronunciation}/vɪlˈkɔmən/+vɪl-+ʋɪl-+-mən+-mn̩+-mm̩}Ⓓ6/69/De-@^.ogg|Adjective}#welcome gl:received with gladness}•Antonym:un@^}•Du bist mir immer '''@^'''.}•You’re always '''welcome''' to my house.}•Das ist eine '''@^e''' Gelegenheit.}•This is a '''welcome''' opportunity.|Usage notes}The German word gern can translate m+:welcome in some constructions. This is not used with a following infinitive:}:Du kannst gern mein Auto nehmen.}•You are welcome to use my car.}The comparative form @^er is rare but possible:}: In Deutschland sind Flüchtlinge nach einer Studie von Amnesty International '''@^er''' als in vielen anderen Staaten.}•According to a study by Amnesty International,refugees are '''more welcome''' in Germany than in many other countries. (Die Zeit,05/19/2016,online)|Derived terms}be@-2nen}@^ heißen}@^ heissen|Interjection}#welcome|Usage notes}''@^'' is construed with prepositions of position (not movement) corresponding to the object. Thus,in with countries and cities,an with bodies of water,bei with people,etc.,as they are generally used to indicate position:}:Willkommen '''in''' Deutschland!}•Welcome to Germany!}:Willkommen '''am''' Bodensee!}•Welcome to Lake Constance!}:Willkommen '''auf''' Helgoland!}•Welcome to Heligoland!}:Willkommen '''auf''' meiner Webseite!}•Welcome to my website!}:Willkommen '''bei''' meinen Eltern!}•Welcome to my parents’ house!}The preposition zu may be used with events and activities:}:Willkommen '''zur''' Weinprobe!}•Welcome to the winetasting!}However,one may also follow the general rule and use bei,auf,or whatever preposition of position is appropriate.|Alternative forms}@-2

*Wotan*German{}|Alternative forms}Wodan|Etymology}Ultimately from Proto-Germanic ⋆Wōdanaz,cognate with from English Woden,from Icelandic Óðinn. Attested since the 12th century in the Latin ''Chronicon'' of Godfrey of Viterbo,where it is spelled ''@^''. In Old High German,the name is attested as from Old High German Wodan.}After Christianization,the name appears to have persisted in folklore and formed various derivations,such as from Old High German Wuotunc,from Old High German Wodunc; from Middle High German Wüetung.}In literary modern German,the spellings ''Wodan'' and ''@^'' competed during the early 19th century,but ''@^'' became prevalent in the wake of Richard Wagner's ''Der Ring des Nibelungen'',published in 1853.}A male given name ''@^'' (also ''Wuotan'',''Woatan'') is attested in Latin beginning in the 9th century. It became obsolete during the high medieval period,but was revived as a rare given name in the 20th century.|Pronunciation}Ⓓ8/8d/De-@^.ogg|Proper noun}(mask.)}#Woden/Odin,a deity of the old Germanic religion,and of modern German reconstructions of this religion}#Given Name

*wurde*German{}|Alternative forms}ward qualifier:archaic}wurd qualifier:colloquial|Etymology}Formed by analogy with the plural @^n,from Middle High German @^n (singular from Middle High German wart). The verbs of this class normally generalise the singular vowel; as in sterben etc. we should thus expect . These forms are attested,but the plural usually retained the ''u''-form and this ''-u-'' tended to be generalised to the singular. A possible reason is the ''a''-forms’ phonetic similarity to war,waren. The final ''-e'' in @^ is unetymological; it goes back to a development in Early Modern German where ''-e'' was added to strong past tenses (after the subjunctive and/or by hypercorrection; hence archaic  for sah,fand). It may have survived here by analogy with the fellow auxiliary hatte.|Pronunciation}/ˈvʊʁdə/}Ⓓc/cd/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ8/85/De-@^2.ogg|Verb}#verb form of [werden]|Usage notes}Until the earlier 20th century,was seen as a correct,but less formal byform of ward. The latter has since become archaic,however.

*wurmen*German{}|Etymology}From t1worm. Formally already in from Middle High German @^ and from Old High German wormōn,but with unrelated senses. Since the 15th century “to have worms,be wormridden”. The contemporary meaning since the later 18th century,seemingly popularised in part by Goethe. Evoking the idea of a nibbling worm in one’s mind or conscience,perhaps remotely based on Isaiah 66:24,Mark 9:44 (“where their worm dieth not”,of the continuous agony and regret of the sinners in hell).|Pronunciation}/ˈvʊʁmən/}Ⓓ8/8e/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#transitive to cause a not necessarily strong but continuous feeling of anger,worry,or regret in someone; to rankle}#}@^ Wenn jemand wider Willen einen Andern unhöflich behandelt,zum Beispiel nicht grüsst,weil er ihn nicht erkennt,so '''wurmt''' ihn diess,obwohl er nicht seiner Gesinnung einen Vorwurf machen kann; ihn kränkt die schlechte Meinung,welche er bei dem Andern erzeugt hat,oder er fürchtet die Folgen einer Verstimmung,...|Derived terms}Wurmen

*Zahn*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German zan,from Middle High German zant,from Old High German zan,from Old High German zand,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆tanþ,from Proto-Germanic ⋆tanþs.}The Old High German nominative ''zan'' alongside ''zand'' is not quite clear,but may go back to an inherited variation that was levelled in the other old languages. The stems ''zan-'' and ''zand-'' were then used indiscriminately in Middle High German. The success of the form without ''-d'' may have been reinforced by the widespread dialectal development:intervocalic ''-nd-'' → ''-nn-'',which produced d-less inflected forms even in dialects that used ''zand-''. Cognates include from Dutch - and from Danish tand,from English tooth. See the latter for more.|Pronunciation}/t͡saːn/}Ⓓ8/8b/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ4/45/De-@^2.ogg}Rhymes:aːn|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[Zähne],diminituve:@^)}#tooth}#fang}#tusk}#cog,tine|Derived terms}Backenzahn}Eckzahn}einen @^ zulegen}Fangzahn}Haare auf den Zähnen haben}Sägezähne}Schneidezahn}Stoßzahn}verzahnen}@^arzt}@^bürste}@^creme}@^ der Zeit}zahnen}@^fee}@^fleisch}zahnlos}@^lücke}@^pasta}@^rad}@^schmelz}@^seide}@^stein}@^stocher}auf den @^ fühlen}steiler @^}@^klempner}Zähne zeigen
